_work.title: Rotulum hieroglyphicum — Wellcome Collection (Individual Illustrations)
_work.blurb: Six individual high-resolution photographs from a Wellcome Collection *Rotulum hieroglyphicum* (English alchemical scroll, Ripley tradition, c.1500–1600): the philosopher bearing staff, two fountain-on-column panels, the golden eagle, the green dragon, and the alchemist holding an alembic. Each is a standalone illustration from a parchment scroll, photographed as a separate IIIF item.
_work.rights: Public Domain. Wellcome Collection open access.
_work.creator: English alchemical tradition (Ripley circle)

entries.title: Alchemist Holding an Alembic (Rotulum hieroglyphicum)
entries.work: Rotulum hieroglyphicum (Wellcome Collection — Ripley Scroll Tradition)
entries.creator: English alchemical tradition, attributed to Ripley circle
entries.medium: manuscript on vellum, pen and watercolor
entries.summary:
The central figure of the alchemist-philosopher holding an alembic — the glass distillation vessel that is the primary instrument of the alchemical laboratory. This image from a *Rotulum hieroglyphicum* ("Hieroglyphic Scroll") at the Wellcome Collection shows the practitioner fully immersed in the Work, holding the alembic at the moment of distillation. The alembic is simultaneously a literal laboratory tool and an emblem of the Work's spiritualizing process: matter rises through heat, becomes volatile, and descends purified. The alchemist's posture — holding the vessel at eye level — suggests not mere mechanistic labour but contemplative *theoria*: the alchemist observes the spirit rising through glass, becoming visible.

## Iconography

The alembic-holding alchemist belongs to the rich visual tradition of the *philosophus*, the wise adept who both labours and contemplates. In the Ripley Scroll tradition, the philosopher-figure opens the scroll's visual program, establishing the unity of practice and theory. The alembic specifically marks the stage of *distillatio*, one of the twelve operations of alchemy catalogued by Paracelsus and earlier authors. This figure appears to be from the same *Rotulum hieroglyphicum* as M0010602–M0010606, forming a suite of individual illustrations photographed from a single English alchemical scroll.

## Significance

The Wellcome Collection's systematic photography of Ripley Scroll witnesses has produced some of the highest-quality public-domain images of English alchemical iconography. These individual panels from a *Rotulum hieroglyphicum* give artists and scholars direct access to the standard visual vocabulary of the tradition. Rampling (*The Experimental Fire*) traces the alchemist-figure tradition across fifty years of English practice.

## For artists & game designers

The alchemist-with-alembic is the archetypal starting character in any alchemy-themed game. This image provides a high-quality template for the practitioner archetype: precise hand-gesture (holding vessel to eye), scholarly dress, contemplative stance. The alembic's shape — bulbous base, tapering neck — is both historically accurate and immediately legible as "alchemy" to modern viewers.

entries.title: Alchemical Fountain on Column — Left Panel (Rotulum hieroglyphicum)
entries.work: Rotulum hieroglyphicum (Wellcome Collection — Ripley Scroll Tradition)
entries.creator: English alchemical tradition, attributed to Ripley circle
entries.medium: manuscript on vellum, pen and watercolor
entries.summary:
The fountain on a column — the *fons philosophorum* or philosophical fountain — is one of the most resonant images in English alchemical iconography. This left-hand panel, from a *Rotulum hieroglyphicum* at the Wellcome Collection, shows the fountain with its column and symbolic accessories; a facing companion panel (M0010603) completes the diptych. The philosophical fountain is the alchemical *bath* where the metals are purified: the fountain's waters are the universal solvent (*menstruum universale*), and the column that supports it represents the axis of the Work, the *columna philosophorum*.

## Iconography

The fountain-on-column motif appears in numerous Ripley Scrolls and was a standard element of English alchemical imagery from c.1480 onward. Its visual sources include: the medieval *fons vitae* (fountain of life) tradition; the Hermetic *Krater* (mixing bowl) of the *Corpus Hermeticum*; and the alchemical bath (*balneum*) described in practical laboratory texts. The fountain here is likely crowned with Sol and Luna medallions (sun and moon), marking the conjunction of masculine and feminine principles in the philosophical water. The column's capitals and decorative elements mark the Work's division into discrete stages.

## Significance

This image is particularly valuable as one of a pair with M0010603 — the two panels together visualize the complete fountain scene, allowing comparison with single-panel versions in other scroll witnesses. The Wellcome Collection's high-resolution photography preserves fine details of the coloring and line work that characterize English workshop production of the period.

## For artists & game designers

The fountain provides a beautiful game environment element: a purification station, healing fountain, or alchemical resource point. The column-and-basin structure is architecturally specific enough to design from — tall central column, wide basin, decorative top with celestial symbols — while remaining emblematic rather than realistic. Works well as a save point or level-transition symbol.

entries.title: Alchemical Fountain on Column — Right Panel (Rotulum hieroglyphicum)
entries.work: Rotulum hieroglyphicum (Wellcome Collection — Ripley Scroll Tradition)
entries.creator: English alchemical tradition, attributed to Ripley circle

entries.summary:
The right-hand companion panel to M0010602, completing the diptych representation of the *fons philosophorum* (philosophical fountain). This panel shows the fountain in its full symbolic context, with the decorative accessories — sun and moon medallions, planetary symbols, inscribed text bands — that annotate the alchemical meaning of the bath. The pair of panels forms a panoramic view of the fountain scene, with the fountain's imagery split between two illustrated sections of the scroll.

## Iconography

Together with M0010602, this panel presents the complete fountain of the philosophers: the source of the universal solvent (*aqua mercurialis*), the place where Sol and Luna meet in conjunction. The symbolic accessories visible in this right-hand panel — likely including sun and moon roundels at the top, planetary signs on the column shaft, and verse text at the base — explain the fountain's role in the Work. The diptych structure is characteristic of Ripley Scroll design: complex, wide images are split across two canvases, requiring the scroll to be unfurled to see the full composition.

## Significance

The paired fountain panels (M0010602–M0010603) are among the most compositionally elaborate images in this *Rotulum hieroglyphicum*, demonstrating the sophisticated visual planning that went into the Ripley Scroll tradition. The Wellcome Collection's separate photography of each panel allows digital reunification of the diptych.

## For artists & game designers

The paired panels are ideal for split-screen or diptych game art: two facing pages of a quest journal, two halves of a loading screen, or two panels of a comic-book-style sequence. The fountain motif recurs across alchemical iconography — cross-reference with the *Splendor Solis* bath scenes for variant design templates.

entries.title: Golden Eagle on a Sphere (Rotulum hieroglyphicum)
entries.work: Rotulum hieroglyphicum (Wellcome Collection — Ripley Scroll Tradition)
entries.creator: English alchemical tradition, attributed to Ripley circle
entries.medium: manuscript on vellum, pen and watercolor
entries.summary:
The golden eagle perched on a sphere is among the most powerful images in English alchemical iconography. This image from a *Rotulum hieroglyphicum* at the Wellcome Collection shows the eagle at its moment of maximum elevation — wings spread, golden plumage fully visible against the sphere beneath it. The eagle represents *volatile mercury* (or the volatile principle of sulphur, depending on tradition), raised above the terrestrial sphere by the heat of distillation and sublimation.

## Iconography

In the Ripley Scroll tradition, the eagle's visual program unfolds in several stages. First, the eagle attacks and is attacked — in some scrolls it appears in combat with the toad (the fixed principle). Then it ascends, marking the stage of *sublimatio*. Here, the eagle stands triumphant on the sphere, marking the completion of the volatile's ascent before the stage of coagulation or fixation brings it back down into the fixed earth. The golden coloring is significant: this is not a raw eagle (the unrefined volatile principle) but a *gilded* eagle — the volatile principle that has absorbed gold through the process of dissolution and is now ready to transfer it to the Stone. The sphere beneath the eagle is the *orbis* or earth — the fixed principle that grounds the Work.

## Significance

The eagle-on-sphere image is one of the most instantly recognizable motifs in Western alchemical iconography, appearing in the Ripley Scroll tradition, the *Rosarium Philosophorum* (1550), and the *Splendor Solis* (1582), as well as emblematic literature from Maier to the Rosicrucian texts. This Wellcome photograph preserves one of the finest colored examples at high resolution.

## For artists & game designers

The golden eagle is a ready-made boss sprite, faction emblem, or achievement icon. The pose — wings spread wide, perched on a sphere — is heraldically legible and compositionally balanced. The sphere beneath adds architectural grounding. Consider this as: (1) the sublimation stage boss; (2) the faction symbol of a volatile/fire alchemical tradition; (3) achievement art for completing the distillation stage.

entries.title: Green Dragon (Rotulum hieroglyphicum)
entries.work: Rotulum hieroglyphicum (Wellcome Collection — Ripley Scroll Tradition)
entries.creator: English alchemical tradition, attributed to Ripley circle
entries.medium: manuscript on vellum, pen and watercolor
entries.summary:
The green dragon is the most menacing figure in the English alchemical visual tradition. This image from a *Rotulum hieroglyphicum* at the Wellcome Collection shows the dragon with wings spread, green scaled body fully displayed. In alchemical symbolism, the green dragon represents *vitriol* (green vitriol / sulphate of iron) or the volatile corrosive principle (*sulphur philosophicum*) that dissolves even gold — the philosophical solvent that initiates the Work by corroding and destroying the impure metals.

## Iconography

The dragon's green color is crucial: it marks the *viridis leo* (green lion / green dragon interchangeability in some traditions), the corrosive principle active in the first stage of the Work. Green is the color of the metal at its most corrosive — the green patina of copper and iron, the green of fresh growth before calcination, the green of vitriol. The dragon's wings mark its volatile nature: it is the *volatile sulphur*, able to rise and attack. Unlike the toad (fixed, earth-bound), the dragon can fly — making it the active, aggressive principle in the alchemical contest. In the Ripley Scroll tradition, the dragon first appears as a destructive agent (consuming the metals) but is eventually overcome, its body transformed into the fixed earth of the Stone.

## Significance

The green dragon / green lion is one of the most powerful symbols in Western alchemy, appearing in texts from Ripley through Flamel through Newton. This Wellcome *Rotulum hieroglyphicum* version is among the finest colored examples available in public domain, with the full green-on-red or green-on-gold color contrast visible at high resolution.

## For artists & game designers

The green dragon is an immediately deployable enemy sprite or alchemical hazard. Its specific design — green wings, scaled body, aggressive posture — is both historically accurate and visually distinctive from generic fantasy dragons. Deploying it as the 'corrosion encounter' or first-stage boss (equivalent to the dissolution stage in the alchemical Work) gives game narrative immediate symbolic depth.

entries.title: Philosopher Bearing Staff with Scroll (Rotulum hieroglyphicum)
entries.work: Rotulum hieroglyphicum (Wellcome Collection — Ripley Scroll Tradition)
entries.creator: English alchemical tradition, attributed to Ripley circle
entries.medium: manuscript on vellum, pen and watercolor
entries.summary:
The philosopher-alchemist bearing a staff with a scroll coiled around it is the quintessential opening image of the *Rotulum hieroglyphicum* tradition — the figure that introduces the entire visual program of the alchemical scroll. This image from the Wellcome Collection preserves one of the finest colored examples at high resolution. The staff-with-scroll is a *caduceus* variant: the staff as Mercury's rod (the universal instrument of transformation), the coiled scroll as the serpent of wisdom (the *ouroboros* in its knowledge form).

## Iconography

This philosopher-figure synthesizes three roles simultaneously: (1) *author* — he bears the scroll of the written revelation, the textual program of the Work; (2) *practitioner* — the staff is the alchemist's instrument, the stirring rod and the pointer; (3) *magus* — the coiled scroll as serpent marks his mastery of transformation. The figure's dress — typically a robe or tabard — marks him as a learned man, not a simple craftsman. His posture — upright, staff raised, scroll held — is an act of *presentatio*: he presents the Work to the viewer, inviting them into the scroll's visual program. This is the gate-keeper image of the entire *Rotulum hieroglyphicum* tradition.

## Significance

The philosopher-figure is the Ripley Scroll's signature opening image, appearing in virtually all surviving witnesses. Rampling (*The Experimental Fire*) analyzes how this opening figure establishes the scroll's claim to authority — positioning the alchemical practitioner as both scholar (holding written text) and adept (commanding the scroll of the Work). This Wellcome example is particularly well-preserved, with detailed coloring of the philosopher's robes and staff.

## For artists & game designers

The sage-with-scroll is the archetype for the alchemist NPC — the quest-giver, the mentor, the keeper of hidden knowledge. The specific pose (upright, staff raised, scroll prominent) is the classic 'sage presenting knowledge' posture. The staff-as-caduceus detail marks him as master of transformation, not merely a laboratory technician. Use as: (1) opening narrator character; (2) quest-giver NPC portrait; (3) character class art for the 'Scholar' or 'Magister' archetype.
